title: Ferns on the Forest Floor
description: Look below the woodland canopy for fern fronds, small mosses, and the structures that produce new growth.
cardDescription: Look below the woodland canopy for fern fronds, small mosses, and the structures that produce new growth.
focus: Ferns and mosses reproduce with spores rather than flower seeds. Their growth forms differ, and the clues separate a reproductive structure from the leaf or stem carrying it.
solvingTip: Use the body part described: a divided leaf, a spreading stem, or a tiny reproductive unit.
words: Tiny reproductive unit produced by a fern or moss
Large often-divided leaf of a fern
Coiled young fern frond before it unfolds
Horizontal stem from which many woodland ferns grow
Spore-bearing case on a stalk in many mosses
Small nonflowering plant forming a soft woodland carpet
Nonflowering plant often bearing divided leaves called fronds
Shelter from direct sunlight beneath forest trees
Slightly wet, as a sheltered patch of forest floor
Anchoring and absorbing organ below a fern's stem
Plant organ represented by a fern's frond
Slender support beneath a moss's spore case
Ground material in which many woodland plants grow
Color of many actively growing fern leaves

answerNotes.SPORE: A spore is not a seed; ferns and mosses have life cycles that differ from those of flowering plants.
answerNotes.FROND: Frond names a leaf form, not the fern's entire body or its underground stem.
answerNotes.FIDDLEHEAD: Fiddlehead describes the curled shape of new growth; the name is not an identification of edibility.
answerNotes.RHIZOME: A rhizome is a stem, even when underground; roots are separate organs growing from it.
answerNotes.CAPSULE: A moss capsule holds spores rather than flower seeds.

title: Acorns Beneath an Oak
description: Explore an oak tree through its familiar nuts, lobed leaves, and woody branches.
cardDescription: Explore an oak tree through its familiar nuts, lobed leaves, and woody branches.
focus: An acorn is an oak’s fruit, usually containing one seed. The clues connect the nut with its cup and the larger tree without treating all oaks as having identical leaves.
solvingTip: Separate the fruit from its covering and from the branch that bears it.
words: Oak fruit often found nestled in a small scaly cup
Cup-shaped structure holding the base of an acorn
Rounded or pointed projecting section of many oak leaves
Tree group whose fruits are acorns
Young tree larger than a tiny seedling
Hard-shelled fruit represented by an acorn
Outer covering of an oak's woody trunk
Woody limb extending from the main trunk
Flat green structure with veins and sometimes deep lobes
Small slender woody shoot at a branch's end
Reproductive structure contained inside an acorn
Cooler sheltered area beneath a broad tree crown
Growth band visible in a cut oak trunk

answerNotes.ACORN: An acorn is a fruit, usually containing one seed; it is not the entire seedling that later grows from it.
answerNotes.CUPULE: The cupule is the acorn's little cup, distinct from the smooth nut sitting in it.
answerNotes.LOBE: A lobe is part of a leaf's outline; not every oak species has the same lobed leaf shape.
answerNotes.OAK: Oaks include many species with different leaves, bark, and growing habits.
answerNotes.SAPLING: Sapling is an informal size or growth-stage term rather than one exact age for every species.

title: A Pine Cone on the Path
description: Study a conifer through its needles, cone scales, and the woody growth around them.
cardDescription: Study a conifer through its needles, cone scales, and the woody growth around them.
subtheme: A Pine Cone on the Path
focus: Pine cones carry reproductive structures rather than forming flowers like a rose. Seed-bearing cones and pollen-producing cones have different roles.
solvingTip: Use the clue’s part or process: leaf, seed covering, sticky material, or airborne powder.
words: Tree group that includes pines, spruces, and firs
Slender pointed leaf of a pine
Sticky substance produced by many conifers
One overlapping segment of a woody pine seed cone
Powdery reproductive material released by male pine cones
Conifer whose familiar leaves are long narrow needles
Reproductive structure associated with a pine tree
Plant beginning carried beneath a pine cone's scales
Protective covering on a pine trunk
Small branch segment bearing needles or cones
Moving air carrying much pine pollen
Hard material forming the trunk beneath its covering
Pointed end of a pine needle
Compact growing point at the end of a shoot

answerNotes.CONIFER: Conifers include familiar cone-bearing trees; the group is broader than pines alone.
answerNotes.NEEDLE: A pine needle is a leaf, not a thorn or a detached cone scale.
answerNotes.RESIN: Resin differs from watery sap in composition and behavior, though the words are sometimes loosely confused.
answerNotes.SCALE: Seed-cone scales protect and carry the seeds; a scale is not the whole cone.
answerNotes.POLLEN: Pollen-producing cones have a different role from the larger seed-bearing cones familiar on the ground.

title: Mushrooms After the Rain
description: Explore visible mushroom structures and the less visible threads growing through woodland material.
cardDescription: Explore visible mushroom structures and the less visible threads growing through woodland material.
focus: A mushroom is a fruiting structure of a fungus. Its cap, underside, and supporting stem have different names, while the thread network can extend through soil or wood.
solvingTip: Read whether the clue describes the visible structure or the hidden network beneath it.
words: Network of fungal threads growing through soil or wood
Single threadlike filament forming part of a fungus
Organism group containing mushrooms, molds, and yeasts
One thin plate beneath the cap of many mushrooms
Microscopic reproductive unit released by a mushroom
Upper umbrella-like portion of a familiar mushroom
Upright support beneath a mushroom's cap
Skirtlike remnant around the stem of some mushrooms
Small opening beneath certain mushroom caps
Material on which many woodland fungi grow
Moist condition often associated with new mushroom growth
Fallen tree section supporting some fungi
Breakdown process in which many fungi take part

answerNotes.MYCELIUM: Mycelium is a network of hyphae; the visible mushroom is only one possible fruiting structure produced by a fungus.
answerNotes.HYPHA: Hypha is singular; hyphae is the plural form often used for the network's individual threads.
answerNotes.FUNGUS: Fungi are not plants and do not obtain energy by plant-style photosynthesis.
answerNotes.GILL: Gills occur in many mushroom forms, but other species have pores or different spore-bearing surfaces.
answerNotes.SPORE: Spores are reproductive units rather than flower seeds; appearance alone is not an edibility guide.

title: Wildflowers Along a Woodland Path
description: Meet woodland flowers through clear names and recognizable plant features.
cardDescription: Meet woodland flowers through clear names and recognizable plant features.
focus: These clues focus on selected plants rather than treating every flower as a garden annual. Common names can describe shape, color, or the time a flower is noticed.
solvingTip: Look for a completed common name or a count of a distinctive flower part.
words: Woodland flower commonly recognized by three petals and three leaflike bracts
Low-growing flower group including purple and white woodland kinds
Common flower name suggesting a blue hanging bell
One colored segment of a flower's corolla
Frond-bearing plant growing beside woodland flowers
Open flower noticed along the woodland path
Green flat plant part beneath a flower
Absorbing organ anchoring a woodland plant
Reduced direct light under woodland trees
Walking route passing the flowering plants
Plant support holding a flower above the ground
Season when many woodland wildflowers bloom before trees fully leaf out

answerNotes.TRILLIUM: The characteristic groups of three help explain trillium's name; the structures below the flower are botanically bracts.
answerNotes.VIOLET: Violet can name a plant or a color; the flower group includes more colors than the name suggests.
answerNotes.BLUEBELL: Bluebell is used for different plants in different regions; the clue concerns the familiar common-name shape.
answerNotes.ANEMONE: Wood anemone is a familiar common-name combination; anemone alone names a larger plant group.
answerNotes.PETAL: Petals belong to the flower itself, while leaves or bracts around it have different roles.
